unit: Ch 5: Acceptance of Deposits by Companies
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Concept and Features of Deposit
explain: A deposit includes any receipt of money by way of deposit, loan, or any other form by a company.
It excludes specific categories of amounts prescribed by the government in consultation with the RBI.
Repayment of a deposit is strictly time-bound and carries an obligation to pay interest.
Deposits can be fully secured by creating a charge on tangible assets or left unsecured.
A company can accept deposits in joint names, up to a maximum of three persons.
Normal deposit tenure ranges from a minimum of 6 months to a maximum of 36 months.

flow.title: Basic Deposit Evaluation Process
steps: Company receives money from person
Check if amount falls under RBI exclusions
If excluded, treat as non-deposit money
If included, classify as deposit
Set tenure between 6 and 36 months
Issue deposit receipt within 21 days

topics.example: An investor gives ₹1,00,000 to a public company for 2 years at 9% interest per annum; this money is classified as a deposit.
remember: Tenure must be between 6 months and 36 months.
Joint deposit holders cannot exceed 3 persons.
mistakes: Assuming partially secured deposits are called secured; if not fully secured on tangible assets, they are classified as unsecured deposits.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of joint holders permitted for a deposit accepted by a company?
quiz.why: Under the deposit rules, deposits can be accepted in joint names not exceeding three persons.

quiz.q: What is the standard maximum tenure allowed for accepting public or member deposits?
quiz.why: Section rules state that no company can accept or renew deposits for a tenure exceeding 36 months.

topics.title: Amounts Not Considered as Deposit
explain: Funds from Central/State Governments, local authorities, or foreign governments/banks are exempt.
Loans from banks, public financial institutions (PFIs), or inter-company deposits (ICDs) are not deposits.
Share application money is exempt if allotment is made within 60 days of receipt.
If share allotment fails, money must be refunded within 15 days, otherwise it becomes a deposit on the 75th day.
Loans from a director are exempt if the director declares in writing that funds are not borrowed from others.
Bonds/debentures secured by first charge on tangible assets or compulsorily convertible within 10 years are exempt.
Security deposits from employees up to their annual salary under an employment contract are exempt.
Business advances for goods/services are exempt if appropriated within 365 days.

flow.title: Share Application Money Deposit Test
steps: Receive share application money
Attempt allotment within 60 days
If allotted, classify as capital
If unallotted, refund within next 15 days
If not refunded by day 75
Treat total amount as deposit

topics.example: A director lends ₹10 lakh to his company after giving a written declaration that the funds are from his personal savings; this loan is not treated as a deposit.
remember: Share allotment window: 60 days; Refund window: 15 days after 60 days.
Employee security deposit cannot exceed 1 year's annual salary.
mistakes: Thinking a director's relative can give loans to a public company without it being treated as a deposit; the exemption for relatives' loans applies only to private companies.

quiz.q: If share application money is not allotted within 60 days, within how many days must it be refunded to avoid being treated as a deposit?
quiz.why: Rule 2(1)(c) mandates refund within 15 days from the expiry of 60 days to prevent it from becoming a deposit.

quiz.q: An employee earning ₹5,00,000 annually deposits ₹6,00,000 as a non-interest-bearing security deposit. How much of this amount is treated as a deposit?
quiz.why: Since the security deposit exceeds the annual salary of ₹5,00,000, the entire amount received is treated as a deposit.

topics.title: Eligible Company and Depositor Definitions
explain: A Depositor is any member who deposits money with a private or public company under Section 73(2).
A Depositor also includes any person from the public who deposits money with an eligible public company under Section 76.
An Eligible Company must be a public company having a Net Worth of at least ₹100 Crore OR a Turnover of at least ₹500 Crore.
An Eligible Company requires prior consent of shareholders via Special Resolution filed with ROC before inviting public deposits.
If borrowings are within limits of Section 180(1)(c), an Ordinary Resolution is sufficient to invite public deposits.

flow.title: Checking Public Acceptance Eligibility
steps: Verify company is a public company
Check Net Worth ≥ ₹100 Crore OR Turnover ≥ ₹500 Crore
If criteria met, company is Eligible
Pass Special Resolution in General Meeting
File resolution copy with ROC
Issue public deposit invitation

topics.example: Apex Public Ltd has a net worth of ₹120 crore. It passes a special resolution in its annual general meeting and files it with the ROC to accept deposits from the general public.
remember: Eligible Company Net Worth threshold: ₹100 Crore.
mistakes: Assuming private companies can become 'eligible companies' to raise money from the public; only public companies meeting net worth/turnover criteria qualify.

quiz.q: What is the minimum turnover required for a public company to qualify as an 'eligible company' under Section 76?
quiz.why: Rule 2(1)(e) defines an eligible company as a public company having a net worth of at least ₹100 crore or turnover of at least ₹500 crore.

quiz.q: Which type of resolution is generally required in a general meeting for an eligible company to invite deposits from the public?
quiz.why: Prior consent by way of a Special Resolution is required before making any invitation to the public.

topics.title: Prohibitive Provisions and Exempted Companies
explain: Section 73(1) prohibits companies from accepting or renewing deposits from the public unless Chapter V rules are satisfied.
Deposit rules do not apply to Banking Companies.
Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) registered with the RBI are exempt from these deposit provisions.
Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) registered with the National Housing Bank (NHB) are also fully exempt.
Central Government can notify any other class of companies to exempt them from Section 73.

flow.title: Applicability of Chapter V Rules
steps: Identify company type
Check if Bank, NBFC, or NHB-registered HFC
If yes, Chapter V rules do NOT apply
If no, non-banking non-financial company
Must strictly follow Chapter V for deposits

topics.example: State Housing Finance Ltd, registered with National Housing Bank, accepts public deposits; it follows NHB regulations instead of Companies Act Chapter V deposit rules.
remember: Exempted sectors: Banking, NBFCs, and NHB-registered HFCs.
mistakes: Thinking manufacturing or trading companies are exempt from deposit rules; Chapter V specifically regulates non-banking non-financial companies.

quiz.q: Which of the following entities is EXEMPT from the deposit provisions of Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013?
o: Housing Finance Company registered with NHB
quiz.why: Housing Finance Companies registered with NHB are explicitly exempted from Chapter V deposit provisions under Rule 1(3).

quiz.q: Under Section 73(1), who has the power to exempt specific companies from deposit restrictions in consultation with RBI?
quiz.why: The Central Government may specify exempted companies in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India.

topics.title: Acceptance of Deposits from Members
explain: A company can accept deposits from its members by passing a resolution in a general meeting.
It must issue a circular in Form DPT-1 to members showing financial position, credit rating, and past defaults.
A copy of Form DPT-1 must be filed with the ROC at least 30 days before its issue to members.
Companies must deposit at least 20% of deposits maturing in the following financial year into a separate 'Deposit Repayment Reserve Account' in a scheduled bank by April 30th each year.
Maximum deposit limit from members is 35% of aggregate paid-up capital, free reserves, and securities premium.
Exemption: Specified private companies, start-ups (for 10 years), or eligible unborrowed private companies can accept up to 100% (or without limit) from members by filing Form DPT-3.

flow.title: Member Deposit Acceptance Steps
steps: Pass resolution in General Meeting
Prepare circular Form DPT-1 with Auditor Certificate
File DPT-1 with ROC 30 days before issue
Send circular DPT-1 to all members
Deposit min 20% maturing deposits in DRR by 30th April
Issue deposit receipt within 21 days of money receipt

topics.example: Beta Private Ltd accepts ₹50 lakh from its members (equal to 100% of its paid-up capital and free reserves). It bypasses circular filing rules under private company exemptions and files DPT-3 with the ROC.
remember: DRR deposit deadline: 30th April each year.
DRR deposit percentage: At least 20% of deposits maturing in the following financial year.
Member deposit limit for normal public companies: 35% of capital + free reserves + securities premium.
mistakes: Using funds in the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account for general business operational expenses; DRR funds can only be used to repay deposits.

quiz.q: By what date must a company deposit funds into the Deposit Repayment Reserve Account each year?
quiz.why: Section 73(2)(c) mandates depositing the required amount into the DRR account on or before 30th April each year.

quiz.q: What is the general maximum limit of deposits a non-eligible public company can raise from its members?
o: 10% of paid-up capital, free reserves & securities premium
25% of paid-up capital, free reserves & securities premium
35% of paid-up capital, free reserves & securities premium
100% of paid-up capital, free reserves & securities premium
quiz.why: Rule 3(3) limits total member deposits outstanding to a maximum of 35% of paid-up capital, free reserves, and securities premium.

topics.title: Acceptance of Deposits from Public by Eligible Companies
explain: Only 'eligible public companies' are allowed to invite and accept deposits from the general public.
Must obtain an annual credit rating from an approved rating agency; rating must be investment grade and filed with ROC in Form DPT-3.
Secured deposits require creating a charge on tangible assets within 30 days of acceptance for an amount not less than the deposit and interest due.
Must appoint one or more Trustees for Depositors and execute a Deposit Trust Deed in Form DPT-2 at least 7 days before issuing advertisement.
Issue circular/advertisement in Form DPT-1 in English and vernacular newspapers, valid up to 6 months from financial year-end or AGM date, whichever is earlier.
Limits: Up to 10% from members and up to 25% from public (Total 35%). For Eligible Government Companies, public deposit limit is up to 35%.

flow.title: Public Deposit Invitation Process
steps: Obtain minimum investment grade Credit Rating
Appoint Trustee and execute DPT-2 deed (min 7 days prior)
File advertisement DPT-1 with ROC (min 30 days prior)
Publish DPT-1 in English & vernacular newspapers
Create charge on tangible assets within 30 days
File annual return of deposits in DPT-3 by 30th June

topics.example: Gamma Ltd, an eligible company, appoints a Corporate Trustee, executes Form DPT-2 seven days before advertising, gets an 'AA' rating, publishes DPT-1 in local papers, and accepts ₹2 crore from the public.
remember: Trust deed execution: Form DPT-2 at least 7 days before issuing advertisement.
ROC filing of advertisement: At least 30 days before publication.
Annual deposit return: Form DPT-3 due by 30th June each year.
mistakes: Creating a charge on intangible assets like goodwill or trademarks to secure public deposits; charge must be created on tangible assets only.

quiz.q: How many days prior to issuing a deposit advertisement must an eligible company execute a Deposit Trust Deed (Form DPT-2)?
quiz.why: Rule 7 requires the company to execute a Deposit Trust Deed in Form DPT-2 at least 7 days before issuing the advertisement.

quiz.q: What is the maximum limit of deposits an Eligible Government Company can accept from the public and members combined?
quiz.why: Rule 3(5) allows an eligible Government company to accept deposits up to 35% of its paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium.

topics.title: Punishment for Contravention of Deposit Rules
explain: If a company accepts deposits in violation of Section 73 or 76, or fails to repay deposits on time, severe statutory penalties apply.
Company Punishment: Fine of minimum ₹1 Crore or twice the amount of deposit accepted (whichever is lower), extending up to ₹10 Crore.
Officer-in-default Punishment: Imprisonment up to 7 years AND fine of minimum ₹25 Lakh extending up to ₹2 Crore.
If default is committed knowingly/wilfully to deceive the company, shareholders, depositors, or tax authorities, action for fraud under Section 447 applies.
Penal Interest: If repayment is delayed on maturity after being claimed, penal interest at 18% p.a. is payable for the overdue period.
General Offense Fine: Fine up to ₹5,000, and up to ₹500 per day for continuing default under Rule 21.

flow.title: Consequences of Illegal Deposit Acceptance
steps: Contravention of Sec 73/76 or non-repayment occurs
Company pays mandatory principal and interest due
Company fined ₹1 Cr (or 2x deposit) to ₹10 Cr
Officer punished with fine ₹25 L to ₹2 Cr AND jail up to 7 yrs
If intent to deceive exists, invoke Section 447 (Fraud)

topics.example: Delta Ltd accepts deposits without filing DPT-1 and defaults on repayment of ₹5 crore. The company faces a fine up to ₹10 crore, and its director faces up to 7 years imprisonment plus fines.
remember: Company fine under 76A: Min ₹1 Crore (or 2x deposit, whichever is lower) to Max ₹10 Crore.
Officer fine under 76A: Min ₹25 Lakh to Max ₹2 Crore.
Penal interest for overdue deposits: 18% per annum.
mistakes: Confusing company fine options; the minimum fine is ₹1 crore or twice the deposit accepted, whichever is lower.

quiz.q: What is the penal rate of interest payable by a company on overdue deposits remaining unpaid after maturity?
quiz.why: Rule 17 specifies a penal interest rate of 18% per annum for the overdue period if the company fails to repay deposits on maturity.

quiz.q: What is the minimum fine levied on an officer-in-default under Section 76A for illegal deposit acceptance?
quiz.why: Section 76A(b) states every officer-in-default shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than ₹25 lakh extending to ₹2 crore.

topics.title: Repayment of Past Deposits Accepted Before 2013 Act
explain: Section 74 applies to deposits accepted before 1-4-2014 which remained unpaid or became due thereafter.
The company had to file a statement of all unpaid deposits and repayment arrangements with the ROC within 3 months.
Past deposits had to be repaid within 3 years from commencement (by 31-3-2017) or before expiry of agreed tenure, whichever is earlier.
The Tribunal (NCLT) may grant extension of time for repayment upon application by the company after evaluating financial conditions.
If a company fails to repay within extended time allowed by NCLT, it is punishable with fine between ₹1 Crore and ₹10 Crore.
Officers-in-default face imprisonment up to 7 years OR fine between ₹25 Lakh and ₹2 Crore, or both.

flow.title: Past Deposit Settlement Workflow
steps: Identify deposits accepted prior to 1-4-2014
File unpaid deposit statement with ROC within 3 months
Repay within 3 years or tenure end (whichever is earlier)
If cash crunch exists, apply to NCLT for time extension
NCLT reviews financial condition and orders timeline
If order defaulted, apply penal consequences under Sec 74(3)

topics.example: Zeta Ltd accepted a 5-year deposit in 2012 under Companies Act 1956. On 1-4-2014, it filed details with the ROC and applied to NCLT under Section 74(2) to repay the deposit as per original tenure maturity.
remember: ROC filing for old deposits: Within 3 months from 1-4-2014.
Mandatory repayment window: Within 3 years or original tenure expiry, whichever is earlier.
mistakes: Believing companies could renew pre-2013 deposits under old terms; any renewal post 1-4-2014 must strictly follow Chapter V of Companies Act, 2013.

quiz.q: Under Section 74(1), what was the maximum time allowed to repay deposits accepted before 1-4-2014 from the date of commencement of the Act?
quiz.why: Section 74(1)(b) required repayment within 3 years from commencement or before expiry of deposit tenure, whichever is earlier.

quiz.q: Which authority is empowered under Section 74(2) to grant an extension of time to a company for repaying pre-existing deposits?
quiz.why: Section 74(2) authorizes the Tribunal (NCLT) to allow further reasonable time to repay deposits after examining the company's financial state.
